title: The state of higher education at the start of the 2026/27 academic year: A personal take on what universities need to get right
summary:

The post The state of higher education at the start of the 2026/27 academic year: A personal take on what universities need to get right appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
As my social media feed fills up with parents posting pictures of children returning to school for the new academic year, as the autumn party conference season gets underway and as Universities UK gear up for their own Annual Conference (taking place next week in Nottingham), it seems the perfect moment to take stock on how UK higher education is faring – and what it can do to control its own future.

So today HEPI is publishing a new Policy Note I have written titled The state of higher education at the start of the 2026/27 academic year: A personal take on what universities need to get right.

As the paper says at the start:

The summer of 2026 turned out to be a politically eventful one, including for higher education institutions. It witnessed a change of UK Prime Minister and a new Secretary of State for Education in Whitehall, the marking of Plaid Cymru’s first 100 days in power in Cardiff and a substantial report from the Future Framework for Sustainability and Success of Scotland’s Universities.

Meanwhile, UCAS reported a record number of 18-year-olds had secured their place in higher education and the media continued to ask questions about the financial sustainability of higher education institutions, the way student loans work and the state of the graduate labour market. Important questions were also raised about the recruitment, oversight and treatment of staff.

This HEPI Policy Note takes stock of some of the key issues facing higher education at the start of 2026/27 and considers what more institutions can do to respond to external pressures and protect their futures. It is based on a speech delivered at the University of St Andrews.

full_text:
Blame the schools. Alan Milburn’s report on Neets, published in May, was one of the most damning comments on the welfare state I have read. It described a new generation of a million mostly poor Britons now encouraged to fare worse, not better, than their parents. This means, said Milburn, that “the great British promise” – the advance of generations – is being broken. A sizeable chunk of the population is going backwards.

The number of young people not in education, employment or training – one in eight of all 16- to 24-year-olds – is rising fast and will be 1.25 million by 2030. More than 80% of them claim to want to find a job, education or training. A third even have “good GCSEs”, but 44% of them are on state benefits, now costing £8.1bn. Many of them suffer from anxiety and other disabilities, according to the NHS. The number of young people with special educational needs has doubled in 10 years. Mental ill-health is bordering on pandemic levels.

The Neets crisis is a gift to politicians. There is always someone else to blame. The most obvious target is Labour’s curiously punitive treatment of small businesses and casual or unskilled jobs. Curbing zero-hours contracts and proposing first-day job security are measures that seem almost targeted at keeping Neets out of work.

But the complaint ringing ever louder from employers is that young people leaving school are unready for work and life in the real world. August’s Department for Work and Pensions survey of employers’ views is an indictment. More than 90% thought the education system should offer more vocational pathways to young people. They pleaded for the young to understand personal motivation, teamwork and time management. They believed schools were too focused on ensuring children and young people passed exams, and lacked anything passing for careers guidance.

Reading these reports leaves an eerie sense of a total mismatch between schools and the social and economic life of the community beyond their gates. They seem like monastic institutions, fixated on their own seasons and periods, and on “subjects” handed down from the past. Above all, they love to measure what they teach, even if it has nothing to do with their pupils’ futures.

If I were an employer I would want new entrants educated in handling money, public affairs, the law, crime and punishment. They should learn about citizenship, the economy and the environment. They should know about public health and their own physical and mental wellbeing. They should be taught elementary ethics and the meaning of morality.

This should be just a beginning. What Neets most clearly lack is self-confidence. The new oracy movement is pleading for practical lessons in getting the young to talk clearly and present themselves to others. They should learn to articulate views and listen to others and learn how to agree and disagree. I cannot imagine a more critical skill, yet it is virtually untaught in schools. The reason, of course, is that authority cannot measure it. There is no league table for confidence.

Here the temperature rises. I used to notice pupils at my local secondary breaking up for the day. They would burst through the gates conversing in twos, threes or larger groups. These groups would merge and dissolve down the street like clouds. I liked to see them as a metaphor for the economy at work.

Today those same groups are quite different, composed of pupils with heads buried in phones and with just a few of them shouting into the air. The American social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, in The Anxious Generation, finds this a universal facet of younger generations on both sides of the Atlantic. Social media is denying them the art of conversation, of intellectual tolerance. It is electronic introversion and there is no GCSE in that – let alone a job interview. These phones must disappear.

Milburn’s Neets report is interim. It poses the problem. We await his solution this autumn. It will doubtless elevate the importance of technical and vocational education alongside the cult of the academic subject. Nothing would aid this more than to end the disastrous merging of universities and technology colleges that took place 30 years ago.

Is it too much to dream that Milburn might look deeper? For more than a century, education’s radicals, such as Rudolf Steiner, Maria Montessori and John Dewey, have sought to bring a fresh relevance to what is taught in schools. Reading, writing and arithmetic remain necessities, but they are primary-stage skills usually acquired before the teens.

Secondary curriculums emerged from the 19th-century academies and have remained little changed ever since. They rank as noble pastimes much to be cherished, but they have scant relevance to the future lives and livelihoods of most pupils. Teaching, the world’s most conservative profession, merely clings to them. Britain’s Neets are the most unjustly treated victims.

title: Reading the Rules for Rule Makers, Part 1
summary:
Reading the Rules for Rule Makers, Part 1 Sara Brady Fri, 09/04/2026 - 03:00 AM Conflating academic freedom with perceived viewpoint diversity: such a fundamental category error as to imply bad faith. Byline(s) Matt Reed Reading the Rules for Rule Makers, Part 1
Sara Brady Fri, 09/04/2026 - 03:00 AM

Conflating academic freedom with perceived viewpoint diversity: such a fundamental category error as to imply bad faith.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
The federal government has issued a raft of proposed changes to the rules for the people who set the rules for colleges and universities. They’re worth taking seriously.

I’ve been reading the Federal Register’s summary of proposed changes to the rules for accrediting agencies, in hopes of eventually helping to craft an institutional comment. I’ll be working my way through this for the next couple of posts. What follows here are my own personal musings, informed by decades of professional experience but not representing my college. I’m hoping that my wise and worldly readers will help me hone these observations into a form more appropriate for an official venue.

In section 602.17, proposed new language would require institutions to “maintain academic freedom protections that are clearly articulated and applied consistently to faculty regardless of appointment classification, race or other immutable characteristics, viewpoint, or ideology.” Yet the very next paragraph requires accrediting agencies to establish policies that would require institutions to “measure student and faculty perceptions on the range of viewpoints and perspectives offered by the institution or program.” Subsequent paragraphs repeatedly conflate academic freedom with perceived viewpoint diversity.

That’s such a fundamental category error as to imply bad faith.

I’ve written before on the fallacy of assuming that there are only two schools of political thought, and on the dangers of hiring people to fit predetermined slots. I stand by all that.

But this proposal is even worse. Start with the measure: student and faculty perceptions on the range of viewpoints offered by the institution or program.

Student perceptions of faculty viewpoints are often catastrophically wrong. I know this from decades of fielding student complaints about professors at several different colleges. Over the course of my own career, I’ve had students say they thought I was conservative, libertarian, liberal and leftist. (Being all of those at the same time would be exhausting, I would think.) I’ve seen them stereotype their instructors based on race, age, gender, clothing, last names, accents, haircuts and all manner of superficial indicators. A professor who goes to the trouble of representing multiple perspectives could easily be misunderstood as endorsing the one a student found most memorable. But according to the proposed language, what matters is not what the professor’s actual perspective is; what matters is what students think it is. If the students are wrong, well, too bad; by this standard, truth is not a defense.

Not that they should need a defense, according to the proffered definition that rules out both viewpoint and ideology as grounds to fire someone. So we’re supposed to ensure some sort of perceived ideological “balance” as defined by local opinion polls, but we’re not supposed to take action to achieve that balance. We’re supposed to achieve the end without using any means.

Even if the goal made sense, which it does not, the simultaneous mandate and prohibition doesn’t make sense on its own terms. In other words, in practice, it means whatever the evaluators want it to mean.

Worse, the standard isn’t only applied to a college or university as a whole; it’s applied to individual programs. So if, say, the HVAC department has two members, and students suspect—correctly or not—both of them of being (gasp) conservative, we would have a lack of viewpoint balance in the program, thereby imperiling the accreditation of the college. I’d have to put out an ad looking for an HVAC person with apparently social democratic leanings, paying them with money we don’t have. Or not, depending on which of the contradictory clauses gets emphasized at any given time. Hence, bad faith.

To give this any credibility at all, I’d need to be convinced that the perceived political leanings of a math professor affect how she teaches calculus. Alternately, I’d expect to see the University of Chicago economics department forced to hire some committed leftists to provide balance.

I’m not holding my breath.

Honestly, though, the ideology part is likely the shiny object meant to distract from the displacement of peer review altogether. For example, the proposed language goes out of its way to emphasize that self-studies shall no longer be required, and that accrediting agencies will no longer have to include or listen to educators. (“Institutions may prefer an independent audit or a review from business leaders in the community …”) In the name of efficiency, accrediting agencies made up of people who have never worked in higher education would be empowered to “conduct a cost/benefit analysis to review and ensure that institutions have sufficient flexibility in instructional staffing policies and policies regarding integrity of scholarly activity.”

That’s worth reading slowly. People from outside higher education will be given the authority to conduct “cost/benefit analyses” to determine whether colleges have sufficient flexibility in firing people. Insufficient flexibility to fire people would be cause to deny accreditation.

In a context of ideological policing, that could get scary.

Stay tuned …

title: 4 Ways Colleges Are Making Support Easier to Access
summary:
4 Ways Colleges Are Making Support Easier to Access Joshua.Bay Fri, 09/04/2026 - 03:00 AM From offering mental health services after hours to putting all essential needs under one roof, colleges are designing support systems around students’ lives. Byline(s) Joshua Bay 4 Ways Colleges Are Making Support Easier to Access
Joshua.Bay Fri, 09/04/2026 - 03:00 AM

From offering mental health services after hours to putting all essential needs under one roof, colleges are designing support systems around students’ lives.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges typically have resources that can help students, but traditional hours, siloed offices, rigid scheduling and awareness gaps can prevent students from using them.

Recent initiatives are trying to remove that friction by bringing support closer to where—and when—students need it.

Here are four things colleges are doing to build support around students’ lives.

Give student parents time to study.

For student parents, time poverty—the lack of discretionary time that comes from balancing classes, parenting and, in many cases, paid work—can make completing a degree more difficult.

Childcare often dominates the conversation when colleges seek to address the demands on student parents. But while access to care can help parents attend class, it doesn’t necessarily address another key challenge: finding uninterrupted time outside the classroom to study and complete coursework.

The University of Louisiana System is testing a new approach to give student parents dedicated time to focus on their coursework while keeping their children nearby. Nicholls State University and the University of Louisiana Monroe have partnered with StudyNPlay, a Louisiana-based program that provides supervised play for kids to free up study time for their parents. Parents can study in a designated space while a supervisor watches their children play nearby and within view.

Katie Dawson, associate vice president for enrollment, innovation and talent strategy at the University of Louisiana System, said student parents can currently use StudyNPlay’s existing off-campus study center in Baton Rouge, while Nicholls State and ULM plan to launch dedicated spaces in partnership with StudyNPlay on their campuses next spring.

“Traditional childcare or babysitting requires you to leave your child somewhere, be it at home or at someone else’s house or facility,” Dawson said. “What StudyNPlay has created is a model that is inclusive of parents having quiet study areas, but also the ability to see their children playing with a supervisor within their own reach.”

Offer mental health care after hours.

For students balancing school with work, family responsibilities and other demands, mental health support, typically offered during traditional campus hours, may not always be available when they need it. The Technical College System of Georgia is looking to close that gap.

In August the system announced a new statewide initiative to expand mental health support across 16 of its 22 campuses. Through a partnership with Uwill, a digital mental health and wellness platform designed for higher education, students will have access to counseling and crisis support 24-7.

Kim Ellis, coordinator of special populations and career services at the college system, said the expansion is designed to remove some of the barriers that can prevent students from seeking support.

Gwinnett Technical College, which began using Uwill in 2024, served as an early test of the model within the system. Ellis said the experience demonstrated that students would use counseling services when they could access them virtually and on their own schedules. At Gwinnett, about 35 percent of Uwill counseling sessions occurred outside traditional campus counseling hours, according to Adam Ring, co-founder of Uwill.

“We were noticing that students would struggle with things like stress, anxiety or not having any way [to] receive counseling services,” Ellis said. “Some of our colleges do have counselors, but not many of them. So we wanted to really look at the student as a whole and see how we could help them not only in the classroom but with things outside of the classroom that may interfere with them coming onto campus.”

Make essential needs easier to navigate.

Colleges and universities offer a wide range of resources designed to help students succeed, but having those supports available doesn’t necessarily mean students know where to find them. For students juggling food insecurity, housing challenges, financial strain or other gaps in basic needs, navigating a web of campus offices can be another barrier to getting help.

Some institutions are trying to eliminate that navigation burden by making it dramatically easier for students to access assistance. Temple University is betting that one way to do that is by putting all essential needs support under one roof.

In August, the public university in Philadelphia opened the Christopher and Julie Barnett Essential Needs Hub, a centralized 26,000-square-foot space that offers students new and expanded resources addressing food and housing insecurity, transportation, clothing, mental and physical health, financial aid, technology access, and other needs.

John Fry, president of Temple, said the hub’s prominent location in the university’s student center was intentional, both to make resources easier to find and to normalize seeking support.

“It’s a space that conveys respect, dignity, access and welcome, and it’s not something hidden away in a corner somewhere where people have to go find it,” Fry said. “It’s right there. It’s out front, and I think the message is that ‘Look, everyone has challenges and struggles. Come here, and this is a community that will serve you.’”

Give student parents the first pick of classes.

For student parents, getting the classes they need isn’t always enough; those classes also have to fit around childcare and other responsibilities. Priority registration can give students more control over that balancing act.

Recent research from Trellis Strategies surveyed nearly 400 parenting students at 49 Texas colleges and universities from mid-June through early July to examine the implementation of two state policies designed to support this population. One of those policies, passed in 2023, requires institutions that offer priority registration to any student group to extend the same opportunity to parenting students.

While the benefit can make a difference for those who receive it, the findings suggest many students don’t know it exists. Some 62 percent of respondents said they did not know whether their institution offered early or priority registration, and 79 percent were unaware that parenting students are entitled to priority registration.

Only 18 percent reported receiving the benefit. But among those who did, 94 percent said the process was easy, and nearly 80 percent said it helped them align their class schedules with childcare responsibilities.

“For a parenting student, the right course at the wrong time isn’t a viable course at all,” said Allyson Cornett, director of research at Trellis Strategies. “It has to fit into the puzzle work of their life and their responsibilities outside of school, and by offering priority registration and letting students take advantage of that, it gives them a better chance to align what they’re doing in school to the rest of their lives outside.”

title: Meet Radha Rajesh, teacher using Messi and real-life stories to explain biology
summary: Biology teacher Radha Rajesh of New Horizon Public School, Bengaluru, has been selected for the National Teachers’ Award 2026, representing CISCE. Known for connecting classroom concepts with real-life examples, she uses cases involving Parkinson’s disease, Lionel Messi and Michael Schumacher to make Biology relatable. Rajesh combines technology, AI, projects and hands-on learning while emphasising critical thinking and source evaluation. Her teaching has earned multiple awards and inspired former students to pursue careers in medicine, research and other fields.
full_text:
How Radha Rajesh makes Biology come alive with Parkinson’s, Messi and Schumacher. (Photo: nhps.in)

What if a Biology lesson on the nervous system began with Parkinson’s disease, a discussion on growth hormones turned to Lionel Messi’s childhood, and a chapter on traumatic brain injuries explored the skiing accident involving Michael Schumacher? For Radha Rajesh, these real-life connections are not distractions from the syllabus. They are a way of making Biology easier to understand, remember and relate to. The Biology teacher and Head of Department at New Horizon Public School, Indiranagar, Bengaluru, has now been selected for the National Teachers’ Award 2026, representing CISCE. President Droupadi Murmu is scheduled to confer the award on 48 selected school teachers at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, on September 5, Teachers’ Day. For Rajesh, the recognition follows years of working to make students curious about science while encouraging critical thinking, independent research and confidence beyond examination marks.

When Biology lessons leave the textbook

Rajesh believes scientific concepts become more meaningful when students can connect them with real people and situations. While teaching the nervous system and synaptic connections, she has used her father’s experience with Parkinson’s disease as a real-world context. During lessons on traumatic brain injuries, the skiing accident involving Schumacher becomes a way to explore the consequences of brain trauma. Similarly, Messi’s childhood experience with growth hormone deficiency provides a relatable context while teaching the pituitary gland and growth hormones. The objective is to move students beyond simply memorising definitions. For Rajesh, a successful Biology lesson is one that makes students wonder about the human body, encourages them to ask questions and motivates them to investigate a subject beyond what is required for an examination.

A family of teachers inspired her

Teaching was familiar territory for Rajesh while growing up. Her grandfather, mother, aunt and uncle were all teachers. She later began voluntarily teaching underprivileged children through her community. Those experiences helped her discover the satisfaction that comes when a child finally understands a difficult concept. She joined New Horizon Public School in May 2014 and gradually took on wider responsibilities, eventually becoming Head of the Biology Department. Her teaching philosophy developed around understanding individual learners and creating opportunities for them to participate, question and experiment.

Using AI and technology without losing human thinking

Rajesh uses animations, simulations, virtual laboratories, interactive quizzes, smart boards and AI-enabled resources to make difficult Biology concepts more accessible. Her classroom also includes project-based activities, hands-on learning, field trips and problem-solving exercises. However, she sees technology as a support system rather than a replacement for independent thinking. With students now able to access information almost instantly, she places increasing importance on teaching them how to question information, analyse evidence and determine whether a source is reliable. For her, the value of technology lies in whether it helps students think more deeply.

Recognition beyond the National Teachers’ Award

The National Teachers’ Award is the latest recognition for Rajesh's contribution to science education. She has received the Teachers’ Insight Award from the U.R. Rao Satellite Centre, ISRO, in 2022, 2024, 2025 and 2026, securing first place each time. She also received the Educator of Excellence Award in 2023. Earlier, she received a Biotechnology Scholarship from the Department of Biotechnology, Government of India, in 1996-97 for academic merit and interest in biotechnology. She also runs a YouTube channel, Radha Rajesh - Biology Beyond the Classroom, where she shares Biology-related videos and shorts.

Her biggest reward comes from former students

For Rajesh, some of the most meaningful recognition has come from students who return years after leaving school. Former students have told her that her teaching influenced their relationship with Biology and, in some cases, their career choices. Some have gone on to become doctors, researchers and other professionals. Her approach is built around the belief that the impact of teaching may not be visible immediately. A concept discussed in a classroom can influence a student's thinking or career years later. As she prepares to receive the National Teachers’ Award, her focus remains on the same objective — helping children feel seen, become curious and recognise their own potential. And perhaps that explains why Parkinson’s, Messi and Schumacher have a place in her Biology classroom: because for her, the best science lessons do not end when the textbook closes.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information and inputs provided by the source. title: From asteroid hunter to Maths wizard, 82 educators to receive National Teachers’ Awards
summary: Teachers who engage in creative pedagogy and community leadership are in focus; among awardees are faculty in Indian Knowledge Systems, including Vaastu Shastra, the Bhagavad Gita, and integrating Sanskrit with AI
full_text:
An asteroid hunter. A Maths wizard. A trailblazer in a coal mining community. A Special Olympics hockey coach. These are among the 82 educators from across the country who will receive the National Teachers’ Awards on September 5, 2026. The President of India Droupadi Murmu will confer the awards.

Among the awardees are 48 school teachers, 21 faculty members in higher education, and 13 trainers from the Union Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. Among the faculty in higher education are proponents of Indian Knowledge Systems, including Vaastu Shastra, the Bhagavad Gita, and the integration of Sanskrit with AI.

One of the awardees, Haryana-based Anil Kaushik, known as the ‘Math Wizard’, built a state-of-the-art physical Maths lab containing over 40 original learning models, alongside a 12-section virtual mathematics lab with 30 ‘Harbans puzzles’. He has co-authored textbooks on Vedic Mathematics and published 22 teaching modules on the national DIKSHA portal.

Divyendu Sen from Rajasthan, another recipient of the award, is a teacher in a government school who bridged rural classrooms with deep-space science by training local students to track and hunt asteroids. He has pioneered low-cost solutions, including an AI-enabled Biology education model, a Virtual Biology Laboratory, and ‘Tree Talk’, a QR-based botanical learning system.

Rajasthan-based teacher Vartika Gulati is an awardee who teaches at the Government Girls Upper Primary School in Jaipur. She turns abstract concepts into everyday experiences — teaching Algebra with groundnuts and geometry with kites. Her initiative, ‘Prashno Se Vigyan’ (Science through questions), replaces rote learning with student-led inquiry.

Odisha-based teacher Padaraj Nayak, based at the Government High School, Alipingal, is receiving the award for guiding students to build over 50 prototypes, including a low-cost automatic plate-washing machine that earned a Government of India patent.

Another awardee, Jharkhand-based Munmun Bhattacherjee, working at the Government Middle School in Barmasia, Dhanbad, Bihar, has spearheaded an institutional turnaround in a vulnerable coal mining community. Aligning with the NEP 2020 and NIPUN Bharat goals, she introduced low-cost Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) tools; integrated Children with Special Needs (CwSN); prevented dropouts through home visits; and guided students toward State arts awards, NEET prep, and vocational independence.

Similarly, Maharashtra-based Kavita Gitte, head teacher at the Sane Guruji Nivasi Vidyalaya in Beed, is being felicitated for spending nearly three decades integrating children of migrant sugarcane workers into mainstream schooling via initiatives like ‘Balrakshak’ and ‘Shikshan Aaplya Dari’. As a national softball and baseball coach, she has also guided nearly 210 students to State and national achievements.

Another awardee, Gujarat-based Nitinkumar, converted a resource-constrained tribal primary school in Vansda, Navsari, into a national hub for digital learning. He built a 45-computer IT lab, a 7D VR/AR lab, an offline ‘Rangpur Server’, and a student journalism studio called ‘R NEWS’. His ‘QR Code Book’ project and ‘Touchable PDFs’ reached over 112,000 students across Gujarat during the pandemic.

Goa-based Mahadev Shinde, who is among the national awardees, is a pioneer in adaptive sports at the Gujarati Samaj Special School, South Goa. Mr. Shinde coached the Indian floor hockey team to four Gold Medals and one Bronze at the 2017 Special Olympics World Winter Games. He served as a Bocce Sports Presenter at the 2023 World Games and has mentored 14 international-level athletes who secured 13 medals for India.

Among the higher education faculty members receiving awards is Kirti Chandra Sahu from the Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad, whose pioneering research on the shape and size distributions of raindrops at different altitudes contributes to more accurate rainfall prediction. “He has developed a unique experimental facility from scratch that simulates atmospheric conditions experienced by raindrops as they descend from clouds to the ground, with potential applications in weather forecasting and climate modelling,” a spokesperson from the Union Ministry of Education said.

Another awardee, Avlokita Agrawal of IIT Roorkee, is a proponent of Vaastu Shastra and ‘Indian Knowledge System in Architecture’ through rational and scientific studies.

Vinay Chamola at the Birla Institute of Technology, Pilani, is receiving the award for the courses he has developed in the Internet of Things (IoT) and drone technology, and for establishing a hands-on IoT Tinkering Lab, translating cutting-edge research into project-based learning. “He also leads an interdisciplinary Shrimad Bhagavad Gita course that has demonstrably enhanced student well-being, blending technical excellence with compassion, values and purpose,” the spokesperson said.

Ankuran Dutta, Head of the Department of Communications, Gauhati University, who has founded Northeast India’s first community and web radio stations, is being awarded for his contribution to participatory communication and cultural outreach.

Another awardee, Shivani V., a faculty member at the Karnataka Sanskrit University, Bengaluru is being felicitated for her work in bridging traditional Sanskrit scholarship with Computational Linguistics, Artificial Intelligence, Digital Humanities, and Indian Knowledge Systems.

“Her research on a computational model for the linguistic study of Sanskrit reflects her pioneering efforts to connect Paninian grammar with modern language technology. She has contributed to major academic and technological initiatives, including Mahakosha, National Language Translation Mission, Shastrakosha, Pythonskrit, and Academic GPS, advancing the digitisation and computational study of Sanskrit knowledge,” the Education Ministry spokesperson stated.

title: Best private student loans for September 2026
full_text:
A college education is probably one of the most expensive purchases you'll make in your lifetime.

The average cost of college today ranges from more than $25,000 to $60,000 per year. With prices that high, it's inevitable that many students will rely on student loans to help fund their education, in addition to their own savings, contributions from family, scholarships, and grants.

Federal student loans are a great first place to start. They typically offer the most competitive rates with fixed APRs and borrower protections. But some students aren't eligible for federal loans, or can't get the full amount they need for school.

As a result, you may turn to private student loans to fill the gap. Here's what you need to know before you apply for a private loan, and some of the top lenders to consider today.

Ascent Funding: Best overall

Our take: Ascent offers several options for undergraduate and graduate student loans with standard repayment terms. We like this lender's longer-than-usual grace period after graduation and its Progressive Repayment option, which allows you to pay a smaller amount when you graduate (similar to some federal repayment plans). Your monthly payment amount increases over time, so you can pay off your loan within the original loan term.

Loan amount: Covers up to the full cost of attendance; overall max of $200,000 for undergraduate and $400,000 for graduate

Repayment options: Interest-only, $25 minimum, full, or deferred payments while in school

Grace period: 9 months for undergraduate and graduate loans

Eligibility: Must be enrolled at least half-time at an eligible university; cosigners must meet credit score and income requirements, but more flexibility for students without a co-signer

Origination or funding fee: None

Co-signer release? Yes, after 12 consecutive on-time payments

Learn more about Ascent's offerings.

College Ave: Best for customer service

Our take: College Ave is an all-around solid private student loan lender based on our criteria. You can cover the full cost of your attendance at an eligible college, and you don't need to be a full-time student. Repayment plans and term options vary, and you'll have the ability to choose your own repayment period. College Ave also encourages co-signers for undergraduates. However, the co-signer release for student loans is longer than other lenders — you'll need to wait until after half of your original repayment term.

College Ave not only offers many of the features we want to see from student loan lenders, but it also has solid online reviews from customers, easily accessible support, and boasts a quick 3-minute application process.

Loan amount: Covers up to the full cost of attendance

Repayment options: Interest-only, $25 minimum, full, or deferred payments while in school

Grace period: 6 months for undergraduate loans, 9 months for graduate loans

Eligibility: Must be enrolled in an eligible school (do not need to be full-time); minimum credit score in the mid-600s for co-signers

Origination or funding fee: None

Co-signer release? Yes, after half of the original repayment term

Learn more about College Ave's offerings.

SoFi: Best for added benefits

Our take: SoFi offers repayment terms between five and 20 years, along with standard repayment plans and deferment options. Like other lenders, SoFi offers forbearance for eligible hardship, but you can also qualify for deferment and reduced repayment options if your circumstances change or you're unable to make payments.

Along with the discount for autopay, you can get an extra bonus for your student loan if you're also a SoFi banking customer. You'll earn up to a $250 one-time cash bonus for a SoFi Checking and Savings account when you have a GPA of 3.0 or higher. Repayment options: Interest-only, $25 minimum, full, or deferred payments while in school

Grace period: 6 months for undergraduate and graduate loans

Eligibility: Must be enrolled at least half-time at an eligible university (may be eligible if you're enrolled less than half-time in your final semester of an undergraduate program); credit score and income affect approval for co-signers

Origination or funding fee: None

Co-signer release? Yes, after 12 consecutive payments

Earnest: Best for long grace period

Our take: Earnest is a good private lender if you want some extra time after graduation before you begin making loan payments, since it offers a nine-month grace period. Earnest also has a well-documented process for entering forbearance during periods of financial hardship and the option for single-month (Skip-A-Payment) forbearance for short-term hardships.

There are some limitations to your in-school repayment options. If you want to make interest-only payments or begin repaying in full while in school, you must have a co-signed loan. Students taking on loans independently can either defer payments or make minimum $25 payments.

Loan amount: Covers up to the full cost of attendance; overall max of $400,000

Repayment options: Interest-only (only for co-signed loans), $25 minimum, full (only for cosigned loans), or deferred payments while in school

Grace period: 9 months for undergraduate and graduate loans

Eligibility: Must be enrolled at least half-time at an eligible university; minimum credit score in the mid-600s for co-signers and students applying independently

Origination or funding fee: None

Co-signer release? Yes, after 12 consecutive on-time payments and providing proof of graduation

Learn more about Earnest's offerings.

Abe: Best payment flexibility

Our take: Abe ranks highly across many of the factors we consider for student loan lenders. It offers a wide range of repayment terms, a long grace period, early co-signer release, and more. When you graduate, you can request a 2% reduction of your principal balance as a Grad Reward, plus you can get up to an additional 0.25% rate discount when you make on-time payments throughout your repayment term (0.05% rate reduction every six months).

What really sets the lender apart is the many protections that Abe offers for borrowers. You'll get protection against default while you're in school, an extra six months of your grace period if you need it, deferment and forbearance options, and the ability to extend your loan term to lower monthly payments if needed.

What is a private student loan?

Private student loans are offered by banks, online lenders, and other financial institutions. They're designed to help you finance your tuition, fees, and other expenses when costs exceed what federal loans and grants may cover or when you don't qualify for federal student loans. You may be able to take on a private student loan for undergraduate, graduate, and professional studies. Some lenders also offer education loans to parents of undergraduates.

Unlike most federal student loans, private student loans require a credit check — and you'll only qualify for the best rates and term options with a solid credit history and income. That's why the majority of private student loan borrowers use co-signers to help secure better loan terms.

Should you get a federal or private student loan?

For most students, it's wise to use all available federal student loan options available to you before turning to private student loan lenders. In fact, many private lenders even encourage students to maximize the federal student loans they qualify for (along with scholarships and grants) before applying for private loans.

Federal student loans are offered by the U.S. Department of Education and are typically either Direct Subsidized Loans, Direct Unsubsidized Loans, or PLUS Loans. Federal loans have fixed interest rates, and those rates tend to be lower than some private student loan rates. However, federal student loans have borrowing limits depending on the type of loan, your year in school, and whether you're a dependent.

Private loans can help cover the amount you need to fully fund your education if you max out your options for federal funding and scholarships. They're also a good option if you're ineligible for federal loans.

However, private loans don't have the same protections and benefits as federal loans, including loan forgiveness programs, income-based repayment plans, lower interest rates, no credit checks, and more.

Read more: Federal or private student loans? Here's the difference

What to look for in a private student loan

Many of the factors we consider when ranking private student loan lenders are also the details you should look for when taking out a loan for your education.

Loan amount: Look for a student loan lender that will cover up to your school's cost of attendance (which usually needs to be certified by your school). This is often the maximum amount you can borrow per year, but some lenders also have total maximum loan amounts. If you need private loans to cover much of your education costs and you plan to borrow over multiple years, this is something to consider.

Repayment terms: Common private student loan term lengths range from five to 15 years, though some lenders offer up to 20 or even longer. The term length you're assigned is important for figuring out how much you'll owe each time you make a monthly payment.

APR: Your student loan interest rate can vary a lot, depending on your credit history, income, and whether you're applying with a co-signer. For private student loans, your APR may be fixed or variable. Use current federal loan rates as a guide to help determine if the private student loan rate you qualify for is competitive.

Repayment options: Income-based repayment plans aren't common for private student loans. Usually, you'll make monthly payments in the amount required to pay down your full loan over your repayment period. While you're in school, you can choose from a wider range of repayment options, whether you want to start making full payments, pay only the accrued interest, make a flat minimum payment, or defer payments altogether.

Co-signer release: Co-signers can be a great way to get a lower interest rate when you apply for student loans. But when you graduate and earn an income for yourself, it can make sense to remove the co-signer so they're no longer responsible for your loan. You'll typically have to make a minimum number of payments toward your loan (12 or 24 consecutive, on-time monthly payments, for example) before you can release your co-signer.

Deferment and forbearance: These options are important protections to consider when dealing with a private student loan lender. Deferment can help you postpone loan payments in certain situations — if you go back to school, take on a medical residency, or go into military service, for example. Forbearance can help pause your loan payments during periods of financial hardship. Options vary, but some lenders offer up to 12 months of forbearance (though interest continues to accrue over that time).

Discharge for disability or death: There's no legal requirement for your private student loan lender to discharge your loans when you die or become permanently disabled, but some lenders do cancel the debt so it doesn't transfer to your co-signer or loved ones. Make sure you review your loan agreement to understand what might happen to your loan after death.

Other benefits: Private student loans may not have as many benefits as federal loans, but some lenders do offer ways to save. Look for discounts for setting up automatic payments (typically a 0.25% interest rate reduction), bonuses you may get for graduating or on-time payments, and more.

Our methodology

Choosing a student loan is one of the most consequential financial decisions a young person will make — often before they have a real sense of what their financial future holds. Our ratings prioritize lenders that offer flexibility and meaningful protections for borrowers who need room to grow into their finances.

We reviewed over a dozen private lenders that offer student loans today. These lenders were scored across nine key categories using data gathered from lender websites, loan agreements, and third-party review platforms, including Trustpilot and the Better Business Bureau.

Categories include APR range (compared to federal loans), fee structures, range of repayment terms, deferment and forbearance options, in-school repayment and grace periods, prequalification and eligibility, and more.

Under our rubric, top-rated lenders are those that are well-reviewed by customers, offer students multiple repayment term lengths and plans, have protections for financial hardship, offer added benefits, and generally give borrowers flexibility over the lifetime of their loans.

title: International education doesn’t need more AI. It needs better decisions.
summary:
"When I first started working in international education nearly two decades ago, success was often measured by one thing — applications. Today, I believe that conversation has changed," writes Rahul Sachdeva.

The post International education doesn’t need more AI. It needs better decisions. appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Universities are no longer asking, “How do we recruit more students?” They’re asking a much more important question: “How do we recruit the right students?”

That shift changes everything.

Across the world, institutions are navigating changing policies, growing compliance expectations and increasing pressure to deliver better student outcomes. At the same time, students expect faster, simpler and more personalised experiences.

The challenge today isn’t attracting more applications.

It’s making better decisions.

This is where I believe technology can make the biggest difference—not by replacing people, but by helping people make more informed decisions.

Too often, our sector has treated technology as another platform or another process.

I think we’ve been asking the wrong question.

Instead of asking, “What can AI do?”, we should be asking, “Where can technology remove friction and create more confidence?”

That philosophy has shaped how we approach innovation at Unizportal.

One area where we saw a clear opportunity was interview preparation.

University interviews have become much more than a conversation. They’re an important part of understanding a student’s motivation, communication skills and authenticity. Yet many students experience this environment for the first time during their actual interview.

That’s not a talent gap.

It’s a preparation gap.

It was one of the reasons we developed ANNIE, our AI-powered interview preparation platform.

The goal wasn’t to teach students what to say. It was to help them understand the process, build confidence and walk into interviews ready to present their genuine potential.

The response from university partners has reinforced something we’ve believed for a long time.

When students are better prepared, universities have better conversations.

And better conversations lead to better decisions.

But for me, ANNIE isn’t the destination.

It’s one example of a much bigger vision.

I believe the future of international education lies in building an intelligent ecosystem where technology quietly supports every stage of the student journey—from helping students make informed choices, to enabling recruitment partners to spend more time advising, to giving universities greater confidence in every admission decision.

None of this replaces human judgement.

It strengthens it.

International education has always been built on trust.

Technology should strengthen that trust, not replace it.

Because I don’t believe the institutions that succeed over the next decade will simply be the ones using the most AI.

They’ll be the ones using technology thoughtfully—to improve quality, strengthen partnerships and create better outcomes for students.

Technology shouldn’t replace judgement.

It should improve it.

And that’s the future of international education I’m excited to help build.

About the author: Rahul Sachdeva is the founder of Unizportal, a global education ecosystem connecting students, recruitment partners and universities through technology-led solutions. With nearly two decades of experience in international education, he is passionate about building trusted partnerships and using innovation to improve student preparedness, institutional confidence and long-term outcomes.

title: Forza Italia vuole premiare solo gli studenti di elitè
summary: Il 7 luglio scorso i senatori di Forza Italia hanno presentato un disegno di legge intitolato “disposizioni in materia di reddito di merito e di incentivo per l’eccellenza per studenti meritevoli”: un “reddito di merito” mensile fra le 500 e le 1000 euro agli studenti considerando – con criteri molto selettivi – il voto del […]
full_text:
Il 7 luglio scorso i senatori di Forza Italia hanno presentato un disegno di legge intitolato “disposizioni in materia di reddito di merito e di incentivo per l’eccellenza per studenti meritevoli”: un “reddito di merito” mensile fra le 500 e le 1000 euro agli studenti considerando – con criteri molto selettivi – il voto del diploma e della triennale, la media ponderata dei voti, il conseguimento dei crediti, la regolarità del percorso degli studi e l’obbligo di partecipare a percorsi formativi e professionalizzanti. Tale reddito, che non terrebbe conto della condizione economica dello studente, è una sorta di premio per il privilegio. È più meritevole lo studente che studia la notte, si cucina e si lava i panni da fuori sede e non ha nessun laureato in famiglia, conseguendo la media del 26, oppure il figlio di papà titolato che ha tutti trenta e potrà assommare alla paghetta mensile quella del governo? L’articolo 34 della Costituzione parla della necessità di garantire ai “capaci e meritevoli” i gradi più alti dell’istruzione, ma specificando: “anche se privi di mezzi”. L’articolo 34 va infatti incrociato con l’articolo 3 (“è compito della Repubblica rimuovere gli ostacoli di ordine economico e sociale, che, limitando di fatto la libertà e l’eguaglianza dei cittadini”). Ma le forze di governo, come si sa, non amano la Costituzione.

Il secondo comma dell’articolo 3 della Costituzione italiana recita che “è compito della Repubblica rimuovere gli ostacoli di ordine economico e sociale, che, limitando di fatto la libertà e l’eguaglianza dei cittadini, impediscono il pieno sviluppo della persona umana”. Contro questo principio cardine del costituzionalismo democratico del secondo dopoguerra, il 7 luglio scorso i senatori di Forza Italia hanno presentato un disegno di legge intitolato “disposizioni in materia di reddito di merito e di incentivo per l’eccellenza per studenti meritevoli”. La richiesta è di predisporre un “reddito di merito” mensile fra le 500 e le 1000 euro agli studenti considerando – con criteri molto selettivi – il voto del diploma e della triennale, la media ponderata dei voti, il conseguimento dei crediti, la regolarità del percorso degli studi e l’obbligo di partecipare a percorsi formativi e professionalizzanti. Tale reddito si aggiungerebbe alle borse di studio erogate sulla base della condizione economica dello studente e dunque non terrebbe conto di quest’ultima. Il fine – dichiara la premessa al disegno di legge – sarebbe quello di “rafforzare il sistema accademico”, “valorizzare il capitale umano” e rimuovere gli ostacoli che determinano la “fuga dei cervelli”. Il contributo sarebbe destinato a coprire i costi della vita universitaria come affitto, trasporti, libri, materiali di studio. Questa proposta si ispira ad analoghi provvedimenti già in via di attuazione nella regione Calabria (Presidente Occhiuto di Forza Italia) e in discussione al Consiglio regionale siciliano, sempre su iniziativa di Forza Italia.

É improbabile che se ne veda l’attuazione, almeno in questa legislatura. Tuttavia è eclatante come i senatori post-berlusconiani non si siano posti il problema dei punti di partenza dei soggetti, così come avevano fatto i costituenti. Questa misura, lungi dal rimuovere gli ostacoli che impediscono agli studenti di rimanere sul territorio a spendere i propri titoli, prefigura una sorta di premio per il privilegio. Innumerevoli studi e statistiche mostrano l’incidenza sui risultati scolastici ed universitari del livello economico e culturale della famiglia di origine. Predisporre un reddito sulla base dei risultati scolastici e universitari, in un quadro sociale così segnato dalla diseguaglianza, significa rinforzare non il diritto allo studio, bensì l’élite: incrementare, cioè, i vantaggi della maggior parte dei beneficiati che in genere dispongono già del sostegno dei familiari. Nessun premio andrebbe invece, ad esempio, agli studenti (e sto pensando a persone in carne ed ossa) che dovendo lavorare regolarmente per mantenersi agli studi non possono raggiungere le medie del 28-30. È più meritevole lo studente che studia la notte, si cucina e si lava i panni da fuori sede e non ha nessun laureato in famiglia, conseguendo la media del 26, oppure il figlio di papà titolato che ha tutti trenta e potrà assommare alla paghetta mensile quella del governo? E se uno studente con media alta si ammala o contrae la depressione e perde il passo, che succede? Perde il reddito? Non si minaccerebbe la solidarietà fra i colleghi, dividendoli fra bravi-ricchi e scarsi-poveri?

Pierre Bourdieu ha spiegato a tutti come i risultati scolastici e universitari per la maggior parte non dipendano dal merito di chi li consegue, ma siano la conferma di una pregressa situazione di privilegio, mentre i cattivi voti vadano viceversa a legittimare l’inferiorità degli altri, senza bisogno (quando va bene) di fare appello all’ereditarietà dell’intelligenza. Con altri strumenti, in Italia, idee affini le aveva rese familiari Don Milani. È vero che l’articolo 34 della Costituzione parla della necessità di garantire ai “capaci e meritevoli” i gradi più alti dell’istruzione, ma specificando: “anche se privi di mezzi”. I padri della Repubblica attingevano alle critiche dei socialisti e di Gramsci al classismo di Gentile: il fine era consentire ai “meritevoli” dei ceti sociali meno abbienti di accedere all’istruzione superiore. L’articolo 34 va infatti incrociato con l’articolo 3. Ma le forze di governo, come si sa, non amano la Costituzione.

(Pubblicato su Il Manifesto)

title: Sotterrare migliaia di mutande per la scienza
summary: Lo ha fatto un gruppo di ricerca per testare la qualità del suolo, rimediando uno degli Ig Nobel, i premi per gli studi scientifici più strani
full_text:
Caricamento player

Sotterrare duemila mutande in giro per la Svizzera aiuta a scoprire l’attività biologica e le condizioni del suolo. Grazie a questo uso poco ortodosso dell’abbigliamento intimo, un gruppo di ricerca svizzero ha vinto un Ig Nobel, i premi che vengono assegnati annualmente alle ricerche più strane e insolite. Il premio è una sorta di contraltare ai Nobel, che vengono invece annunciati a inizio ottobre.

La ricerca sulle mutande, e altre su come trasformare le proboscidi delle zanzare in stampanti 3D e su come soffiarsi al meglio il naso, sono state premiate giovedì durante una cerimonia densa di scienza e gag nerd. Gli Ig Nobel (dal gioco di parole con la parola inglese “ignoble”, cioè ignobile) sono stati consegnati a Zurigo, in Svizzera, e non a Boston negli Stati Uniti come avveniva di solito.

Lo spostamento si è reso necessario a causa delle forti limitazioni imposte dall’amministrazione Trump per chi proviene da diverse parti del mondo. L’anno scorso quattro dei dieci vincitori avevano preferito non partecipare alla premiazione proprio per evitare rischi col loro viaggio negli Stati Uniti.

Nello spirito umoristico dell’iniziativa, il gruppo di ricerca dello studio sulle condizioni del suolo si è presentato sul palco con una portabandiera che sventolava alcune mutande usate nell’esperimento e un ricercatore travestito da insetto. Per il loro studio, i ricercatori avevano inviato a mille volontari in Svizzera due mutande di cotone, da seppellire in modo da osservare come la cellulosa che costituiva il tessuto veniva decomposta da batteri, funghi e altri organismi presenti nel suolo. Il metodo è stato poi messo a confronto con quello delle bustine da tè, che vengono già usate per questo tipo di test.

A ogni volontario era stato richiesto di lasciare una mutanda sotterrata per 30 giorni e un’altra per 60, e di rispedirle poi ai ricercatori con un campione di suolo. L’analisi ha rilevato che le mutande tendono a decomporsi più rapidamente nei giardini privati, dove è presente più materia organica. Nei prati rasati l’attività degli organismi al suolo era invece inferiore, mentre nei campi agricoli e nei prati naturali si collocava nel mezzo. Il gruppo di ricerca ha inoltre notato che il livello di sbrindellamento delle mutande dipendeva dalla temperatura del suolo, dall’umidità e da altre variabili come la quantità di nutrienti.

Lo studio ha infine concluso che una mutanda di cotone può diventare uno strumento scientifico per capire quanto è attivo biologicamente un terreno. Si dovrebbe però avere una mutanda standard, sempre uguale come quelle dell’esperimento, per ridurre le variabili, nel caso di analisi su scala globale.

Un gruppo di ricerca in Canada è stato invece premiato per avere sviluppato un ugello microscopico per le stampanti 3D sfruttando la proboscide di una zanzara. È una parte piccolissima, ma complessa: deve riuscire a perforare la pelle, raggiungere i vasi sanguigni e aspirare il sangue. Montandola su una apposita stampante 3D il gruppo di ricerca è riuscito a depositare materiale con una risoluzione di circa 20 micrometri (un micrometro è un milionesimo di metro), circa la metà rispetto a quanto si può ottenere con gli ugelli metallici attualmente disponibili. Una parte biologica minuscola e facilmente reperibile potrebbe sostituire componenti più costosi e dare la possibilità di stampare oggetti molto piccoli, utili per la ricerca medica e per i prodotti elettronici.

È un esempio di “necrobotica”, cioè l’impiego di parti di animali morti per costruire dispositivi robotici. Prima di arrivare alle zanzare, il gruppo di ricerca aveva fatto esperimenti con diversi altri insetti. Sul palco degli Ig Nobel, uno degli autori dello studio si è presentato con una zanzara di pezza sulla spalla.

Altri ricercatori hanno ritirato il premio con cappelli a forma di scarafaggio e t-shirt con la scritta “Lo scarafaggio è il mio animale guida”. Hanno scoperto che le proteine del latte prodotte da una specie di scarafaggio (Diploptera punctata) sono tre volte più caloriche di quelle presenti nel latte vaccino. La specie studiata è vivipara, quindi gli embrioni si sviluppano nel corpo della madre e vengono nutriti con una sorta di latte prodotto nella camera di covata dello scarafaggio. È molto concentrato e nutriente in modo da fornire un’alimentazione continua ed efficiente per lo sviluppo dei nuovi scarafaggi.

Un altro gruppo di ricerca è stato premiato per avere provato a capire che cosa induce o meno le vipere a mordere gli umani, scoprendo che le probabilità aumentano se viene pestata loro la testa (la metodologia è stata contestata e lo studio ritirato). I ricercatori che si sono presentati con dei grandi impermeabili gialli hanno invece illustrato come deve essere progettato un orinatoio a muro per minimizzare gli schizzi di ritorno. Hanno sviluppato Nautilus (o Nauti-loo, nello slang inglese loo indica il gabinetto), un orinatoio ispirato alla conchiglia del nautilo che azzera quasi completamente gli schizzi, favorendo un angolo di incidenza della pipì a 30 gradi.

A differenza dei Nobel, agli Ig Nobel possono essere premiate anche persone morte. Quest’anno un premio è stato assegnato postumo al ricercatore giapponese Tokuji Unno che studiò a lungo e in modo dettagliato il modo migliore per soffiarsi il naso. Concluse che più forte è il getto d’aria che si produce, più efficacemente si elimina il muco, senza che ci siano comunque rischi per la pressione nell’orecchio.

Un altro gruppo di ricerca è stato premiato per uno studio che aveva l’obiettivo di capire se il livello socioeconomico influenzi la propensione a comportarsi in modo scorretto. In diversi esperimenti, hanno confrontato il comportamento delle persone per capire se chi apparteneva alle classi più alte fosse più propenso a tagliare la strada alle auto e ai pedoni, a prendere per sé delle caramelle destinate ai bambini e a mentire. In tutti gli esperimenti le persone con status più elevato si sono mostrate più inclini a comportamenti non etici e legati all’avidità. Gli autori hanno però chiarito che si tratta ovviamente di una tendenza, non di una regola: esistono persone ricche molto altruiste.

Tra gli altri premiati ci sono stati gli autori di una ricerca sui genitori che trovano piacevole l’odore dei loro figli quando sono piccoli e quelli di uno studio sulle preferenze in termini di amici: li preferiamo gentili e affidabili, ma apprezziamo che siano aggressivi e mal disposti verso le persone che consideriamo nemiche. Infine un Ig Nobel è stato assegnato a un gruppo di ricerca che ha proposto una definizione di bacio che sia valida non solo per gli umani, ma anche per gli altri animali: «Interazione non agonista che implica un contatto orale intraspecifico e mirato, con un certo movimento delle labbra/apparati boccali e senza trasferimento di cibo».

Questa è la 36esima edizione degli Ig Nobel. Furono inventati dalla rivista umoristica statunitense Annals of Improbable Research, che pubblica articoli scientifici reali, per quanto insoliti, e altri inventati e a scopo umoristico. I premi vengono annunciati ogni anno con la medesima spiegazione: «Molta buona scienza viene attaccata per il suo essere assurda. Molta cattiva scienza viene celebrata nonostante sia assurda».

La cerimonia densa di umorismo e scherzi in cui vengono assegnati gli Ig Nobel porta spesso a sottovalutare il potenziale delle ricerche che vengono premiate, che a modo loro possono comunque portare a nuove scoperte e all’avanzamento della conoscenza. Non è insolito che alcune grandi scoperte vengano fatte proprio partendo da piccoli studi o idee balzane, contenenti però dati e osservazioni utili per portare avanti nuove ricerche.

La novità di quest’anno è stata soprattutto il trasferimento della cerimonia dagli Stati Uniti all’Europa. Dopo Zurigo, l’anno prossimo la premiazione si terrà ad Anversa, in Belgio, poi sarà nuovamente ospitata a Zurigo nel 2028. Al momento non è previsto un ritorno a Boston, come aveva già annunciato lo scorso marzo il “maestro delle cerimonie” del premio, Marc Abrahams: «Nell’ultimo anno per i nostri ospiti è diventato poco sicuro visitare il paese. Onestamente non possiamo chiedere ai nuovi vincitori, o ai giornalisti che si occuperanno dell’evento, di viaggiare verso gli Stati Uniti quest’anno».

Gli ultimi due anni sono stati difficili per diversi ambiti della ricerca scientifica statunitense, a causa dei tagli ai finanziamenti federali decisi dall’amministrazione Trump e con una crescente incertezza per università e ricercatori. A questo si aggiungono le politiche sull’immigrazione e le nuove restrizioni per chi vuole entrare nel paese, che stanno rendendo più complicato per scienziati e studenti stranieri lavorare o studiare negli Stati Uniti, con il rischio di indebolire nel tempo la competitività scientifica del paese e il ruolo che ha avuto per decenni nella ricerca internazionale.

Το άρθρο Το ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. συμμετέχει στην 90ή ΔΕΘ: Με το βλέμμα στο μέλλον της έρευνας και της καινοτομίας εμφανίστηκε πρώτα στο Hellenic Foundation research and innovation.
full_text:
Το Ελληνικό Ίδρυμα Έρευνας και Καινοτομίας (ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.) εγκαινιάζει τη νέα εποχή του παραγωγικού μετασχηματισμού της έρευνας και της επένδυσης στην καινοτομία, με τη συμμετοχή του στην 90ή Διεθνή Έκθεση Θεσσαλονίκης. Στο πλαίσιο αυτής της παρουσίας, θα παρουσιαστεί ο στρατηγικός σχεδιασμός των δράσεων για την περίοδο 2026–2030, ο οποίος θα εξειδικευτεί περαιτέρω σε συνεργασία με το Υπουργείο Ανάπτυξης και το σύνολο του ελληνικού οικοσυστήματος έρευνας και καινοτομίας. Ο σχεδιασμός αυτός διέπεται από τις θεμελιώδεις αρχές της διαφάνειας και αξιοκρατίας στην αξιολόγηση, στοχεύοντας στην εξασφάλιση και διεύρυνση του αντικτύπου, στην ωρίμανση της έρευνας και στην αξιοποίηση των αποτελεσμάτων της προς την κατεύθυνση της καινοτομίας.

Στο πλαίσιο των εκδηλώσεων του Υπουργείου Ανάπτυξης στο Περίπτερο 7, το Σάββατο 5 Σεπτεμβρίου 2026, στις 15:00, θα πραγματοποιηθεί εκδήλωση με τίτλο: «ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. Εγκαινιάζοντας τη Νέα Εποχή – από το ορόσημο της δεκαετούς στήριξης της έρευνας στην νέα εποχή του παραγωγικού μετασχηματισμού της έρευνας και της επένδυσης στην καινοτομία». Η εκδήλωση θα μεταδοθεί ζωντανά μέσα από τα επίσημα κανάλια του Υπουργείου Ανάπτυξης στο Facebook και στο YouTube.

Στην εκδήλωση θα συμμετάσχουν οι εξής ακόλουθοι:

Σταύρος Καλαφάτης, Υφυπουργός Ανάπτυξης,

Νίκος Παπαϊωάννου, Υφυπουργός Παιδείας, Θρησκευμάτων και Αθλητισμού,

Δρ. Δημήτρης Τερζής, Γενικός Γραμματέας Έρευνας και Καινοτομίας,

Ευστράτιος Σιμόπουλος, Πρόεδρος της Κοινοβουλευτικής Επιτροπής Έρευνας και Τεχνολογίας,

Ευάγγελος Μπεκιάρης, Πρόεδρος Δ.Σ. του ΕΚΕΤΑ,

Χαράλαμπος Μπιλλίνης, Πρύτανης του Πανεπιστημίου Θεσσαλίας,

Κατερίνα Πραματάρη, Partner της Uni.Fund και Καθηγήτρια στο Οικονομικό Πανεπιστήμιο Αθηνών,

Γεωργία Ανδρέου, Πρόεδρος του Επιστημονικού Συμβουλίου του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.,

Δημήτρης Βέργαδος, Πρόεδρος της Γενικής Συνέλευσης του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.,

Γιώργος Καρυδάκης, Διευθυντής του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.

Η απόφαση του Υπουργείου Ανάπτυξης για την ένταξη του Στρατηγικού Προγραμματισμού του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ., για την περίοδο 2026-2030, στο Τομεακό Πρόγραμμα Ανάπτυξης (ΤΠΑ) αποδεικνύει την διαχρονική, έμπρακτη και ουσιαστική στήριξή της Πολιτείας στο ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.. Ταυτόχρονα, διασφαλίζει τη χρηματοδότησή του για την επόμενη προγραμματική περίοδο, διαμορφώνοντας ένα σταθερό πλαίσιο για τη συνέχιση της αποστολής του Ιδρύματος προς όφελος της ερευνητικής κοινότητας της χώρας και του παραγωγικού μετασχηματισμού της έρευνας.

Παράλληλα, το κομβικό ορόσημο της συμπλήρωσης δέκα ετών από την ίδρυση του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. επιβεβαιώνει τη διαχρονική ενίσχυση της επιστημονικής αριστείας και σηματοδοτεί την εδραίωση του Ιδρύματος ως κεντρικού πυλώνα του εθνικού οικοσυστήματος έρευνας και καινοτομίας. Η παρουσία του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. στην επετειακή 90ή ΔΕΘ αποτελεί αφορμή για μια αναδρομή στους σημαντικότερους σταθμούς της δεκαετούς πορείας του, αναδεικνύοντας το έργο και τον αντίκτυπό του στην επιστημονική κοινότητα και την κοινωνία.

This design is governed by the fundamental principles of transparency and meritocracy in evaluation, aiming to ensure and expand the impact, to mature research and to exploit its results in the direction of innovation.

The following will participate in the event:

Stavros Kalafatis, Deputy Minister of Development,

Nikos Papaioannou, Deputy Minister of Education, Religious Affairs and Sports,

Dr. Dimitris Terzis, Secretary General of Research and Innovation,

Efstratios Simopoulos, President of the Parliamentary Committee for Research and Technology,

Evangelos Bekiaris, Chairman of the Board of Directors of EKETA,

Charalambos Billinis, Rector of the University of Thessaly,

Katerina Pramatari, Partner of Uni.Fund and Professor at the Athens University of Economics and Business,

Georgia Andreou, President of the Scientific Council of EL.ID.EK.,

Dimitris Vergados, President of the General Assembly of EL.ID.EK.,

Giorgos Karydakis, Director of EL.ID.EK.
